summary: Defines requirements and a framework for using GMPLS in multi-region and multi-layer networks, where several switching technologies are controlled together. A region is a switching technology domain and a multi-layer network may have one or several. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine one traffic office running roads, rails, and boats together. This paper lists what is needed to manage networks with several kinds of switching.

subtitle: How to manage networks with multiple switching technologies under one control plane

tldr.problem: Large networks often have multiple switching technologies (packet routing, Layer 2 switching, TDM, wavelength switching) operated independently, requiring separate control planes and management systems. This creates complexity, inefficiency, and missed opportunities for cross-layer resource optimization.
tldr.mechanism: GMPLS (Generalized MPLS) provides a single unified control plane that can manage multiple switching types simultaneously. Regions represent switching technology domains (PSC, L2SC, TDM, LSC, FSC). Multiple data plane layers can exist within a single region. Lower-layer LSPs can be advertised as TE links to upper layers.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defines requirements and a framework for GMPLS-based multi-layer and multi-region networks without prescribing specific protocol solutions. It enables unified resource management, simplified service provisioning, and better optimization across all layers.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Single control plane instance per MLN/MRN

today: RFC 5212 remains the authoritative requirements document for GMPLS multi-region and multi-layer networks. These architectures are deployed in operator networks for managing diverse switching technologies under unified control. The requirements documented here guided the development of subsequent protocol specifications. The framework supports modern network architectures where packet, optical, and other switching technologies operate together under automated control.

sections.title: The Case for Multi-Layer Control
sections.content:
GMPLS extends MPLS to handle multiple switching technologies: Packet Switching Capable (PSC), Layer-2 Switching Capable (L2SC), Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM), Lambda Switching Capable (LSC), and Fiber Switching Capable (FSC). Each switching type is called a region, and the associated control plane instance manages that region. A layer is a data plane switching granularity level (e.g., VC4, VC-12 in TDM). Multiple layers can exist in one region.

A multi-region network (MRN) supports at least two different switching types, either on the same device (hybrid node) or different devices, controlled by a single GMPLS instance. A multi-layer network (MLN) more broadly covers any network with multiple data plane layers controlled by one GMPLS instance.

The benefits of unified control are substantial: one control plane instance reduces complexity and processing load; one addressing space eliminates duplicate identifiers; one routing protocol and TE database per router eliminates the need for a mesh of routing adjacencies per layer; unified traffic engineering allows path computation and resource optimization across all layers simultaneously; rapid service provisioning across all technologies.
sections.eli5: If one manager controls roads, rails, and boats, they can route packages more efficiently. They do not need to maintain separate maps for each. They can use a boat underneath to create a road across a river. One plan works for everything instead of coordinating three separate plans.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Network Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines several key concepts. An Interface Switching Capability (ISC) is the ability to switch a particular data plane technology (e.g., packet, TDM). ISC values are advertised in Interface Switching Capability Descriptors (ISCDs), which also include encoding type and bandwidth granularity.

Network nodes are classified as single-switching-type-capable (supports one ISC per interface) or multi-switching-type-capable. Multi-switching-type-capable nodes can be simplex (different ISCs on separate interfaces) or hybrid (different ISCs on the same interface with internal adjustment capability).

Forwarding Adjacency LSPs (FA-LSPs) are lower-layer LSPs that are advertised as TE links to upper layers. This allows higher-layer LSPs to be nested over lower-layer paths. Virtual Network Topology (VNT) is the set of TE links (real or virtual) advertised by the lower layer that represents available paths for upper-layer routing.

The RFC distinguishes vertical interaction (collaboration between layers within a node) from horizontal interaction (protocol exchanges between nodes within a layer).
sections.eli5: Each interface can support one or more switching types. A router can either keep different switching types completely separate, or use internal connections to convert traffic from one type to another. A lower-layer path can be advertised as a link to the upper layer, hiding the complexity of how it is implemented underneath.

sections.title: Core Requirements and Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC lists functional requirements for GMPLS protocols supporting MLN/MRN. Path computation must handle any combination of single-type and multi-type-capable nodes, including routes that span multiple layers or regions. Scalability is critical: the TE database contains links from all layers of all regions, potentially requiring aggregation via VNTs to manage size. Path computation time matters for network restoration. Stability requires smooth VNT changes without destabilizing upper layers. Disruption minimization means traffic should not be interrupted unnecessarily when reconfiguring lower-layer FA-LSPs.

LSP attribute inheritance ensures TE parameters (TE metric, bandwidth limits, protection attributes, SRLGs) are correctly propagated from lower layers to FA-LSPs. Nested signaling refers to the ability to establish higher-layer LSPs that trigger automatic setup of lower-layer FA-LSPs when needed. Resource utilization requires optimizing FA-LSP setup and release to avoid wasting lower-layer capacity.

Virtual TE links allow advertising potential lower-layer paths without pre-establishing the underlying LSPs, reducing bandwidth waste while keeping upper-layer topology stable.
sections.eli5: The system must be able to route a packet through multiple switching types, finding the best path across all of them. The routing tables can get very large, so the system should hide unnecessary details. When an upper layer needs a path through a lower layer, it might automatically create that path on the fly. Old paths should be cleaned up when no longer needed, and the system should not waste bandwidth keeping paths alive if they are not being used yet.

sections.title: Management and Operations
sections.content:
An MLN can be managed in different ways. Some operators prefer per-layer management entities, maintaining separate management systems for each layer that coordinate via the boundary nodes. This requires management systems to track when triggered signaling creates new LSPs in the layer. Others prefer cross-layer management using a unified management system that understands all layers, or a meta-management system that coordinates separate management tools.

When layer boundaries coincide with administrative boundaries (different operators), unified management is unlikely. Instead, the lower-layer management system reports on resource availability and alarms to the upper layer, with some information sharing between administrations to facilitate operation.

The RFC emphasizes that Operations and Management (OAM) mechanisms are important. End-to-end OAM must work across layer boundaries, with client-layer OAM operations mapped to server-layer OAM where technologies differ. Status, errors, and alarms from the server layer must be available to the client layer. Configuration should be subject to policy so the lower layer can filter or hide details as appropriate.
sections.eli5: Someone must oversee the whole multi-layer network. This could be one person managing everything, separate teams coordinating with each other, or teams from different companies sharing limited information if they operate different layers. The system must check that paths work end-to-end across all layers and report problems up the chain.

sections.title: Framework and Next Steps
sections.content:
This RFC provides the foundation and requirements for GMPLS-based multi-region and multi-layer networks. It does not specify protocol details or solutions; those are addressed in separate implementation documents and applicability statements. The framework enables service providers to build networks where diverse switching technologies operate under unified control, allowing efficient resource usage, rapid provisioning, and optimized traffic engineering across all layers and regions simultaneously.

The requirement for per-layer OAM mapping, virtual TE link management, FA-LSP release policies, and stability mechanisms ensure that the benefits of unified control can be achieved without introducing operational complexity or service disruptions. The architecture remains flexible, allowing solutions ranging from tightly coupled unified management to loosely coordinated separate management systems.
sections.eli5: This document lays out the big picture: what a unified multi-layer network needs to do. It does not say exactly how to do it—that is for other documents to specify. As long as the system meets these requirements, different vendors can implement it different ways and it will still work together.
